title: Purchase of 84 Frederick Street for shelter
subtitle: Also: Kitchener airport height rules, budget sub-committee, arts grants, Fischer-Hallman road tender, wastewater surveillance advocacy.
overview: Regional Council agreed to buy 84 Frederick Street in Kitchener from the YWCA for $6.5 million, with $9.464 million in debenture financing that includes initial capital renewal {{vote:m15}}. Staff said the purchase would stabilize the shelter system as the King Street shelter lease ends. A separate operating plan, to be developed with community partners and the City of Kitchener, will return to Council.

Council also approved most of Kitchener's Official Plan amendments but modified Amendment 49 to protect flight paths at the Region of Waterloo International Airport. It rejected Kitchener's version, which relied on holding provisions {{vote:m23}}, and approved the staff-recommended version {{vote:m24}}. The Region also set a budget direction aiming for an increase below 8 per cent {{vote:m12}} and formed a volunteer sub-committee to review the budget {{vote:m28}}.

Other decisions included a $11.575 million tender for Fischer-Hallman/Bearinger Road improvements, $306,000 in arts and culture grants including the Fashion History Museum, and advocacy to the provincial and federal governments on addictions services and wastewater surveillance. A request for emergency funding for THEMUSEUM was defeated {{vote:m27}}.

decisions.detail: Council authorized buying 84 Frederick Street, Kitchener, from the YWCA for $6.5 million and approved $9.464 million in debentures for the purchase and initial capital renewal {{vote:m15}}.
Council approved Amendment 49 with the staff-recommended modifications to protect airport flight paths, after Kitchener's original version was defeated {{vote:m24}}.

Council directed staff to return with a budget under an 8 per cent tax rate increase and to review external funding, mandated services and administrative costs, and approved up to $90,000 in Community Environmental Fund grants and a 2025 compensation review {{vote:m12}}.
Council created a volunteer sub-committee to work with staff on reviewing the budget before the first 2025 budget committee meeting {{vote:m28}}.
Council accepted Sierra Infrastructure's $11,575,000 plus taxes tender for improvements from Columbia Street West to Westmount Road North in Waterloo.
Council approved $306,000 in 2024 grants, and a proposal to defer the Fashion History Museum's $29,500 until a legal agreement with Cambridge was defeated {{vote:m20}}.
Council approved the negotiated $4,005,223.20 plus taxes acquisition from Miovision Technologies for the TrafficLink system and advanced $1,064,000 in capital funding from 2025 to 2024.
Council resolved to advocate that the federal government include Waterloo Region as a sampling site in its wastewater surveillance program {{vote:m32}}.

debate: On 84 Frederick Street, staff said a permanent owned site would end the disruption of temporary shelters, and some councillors saw it as part of the plan to end chronic homelessness. One councillor opposed the purchase over concerns about neighbourhood effects without a set operating plan. Kitchener's representatives raised concerns about the concentration of services downtown and asked why the former police building at 134 Frederick Street was not used. Staff said that building is unsuited to shelter use.

On Amendment 49, a delegate for developers and Kitchener's representatives argued that holding provisions achieve the same protection as height limits with less cost and delay. Regional staff said that once a hold is lifted, nothing regulates height in the zoning by-law. A later owner could seek more height and appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Staff also said recent navigation changes and taller buildings made a maximum height necessary.

On the Fashion History Museum grant, supporters of deferral said the Region should not fund an organization with an unresolved lease dispute with Cambridge. Opponents said the museum met the Region's criteria and that the Region should not be leveraged into a municipal dispute. Staff noted the museum is not insolvent but its 2023 audit was not yet available.

Two delegates urged Council to keep local wastewater monitoring after the provincial program ends. Public health staff said continuing it locally would cost several times more than figures quoted elsewhere, and a councillor's motion sought federal inclusion instead.

On the budget sub-committee and addictions motion, some councillors wanted deeper cost reductions in areas of provincial responsibility. Others asked for more concrete proposals on treatment needs, and staff said the mental health action table would define them.
